1  Introduction
Stricter regulations, quality seals and increasing require-
ments on raw material purities have led to the closer look 
on possible dangerous substances in products used in 
plastics applications. Thereby, Polycyclic Aromatic Hydro-
carbons (PAHs) have been identifi ed as possible danger-
ous substances, resulting in the essential requirement to 
be eliminated at best in raw materials. Orion Engineered 
Carbons focuses on the development of safer products, in 
particular on those, which are related to food- and skin-
contact, to support the manufacturing of safe goods. The 
increasing knowledge on those substances together with 
the improvements of the analytical methods generate a 
detailed understanding. This brochure will present the 
fi ndings by clarifying the diff erent PAH regulations on your 
individual application needs.
2.1.1 Commission Regulation (EU) No. 10/2011 
(European Food Contact Regulation)
“Carbon black” , FCM*-substance No. 411, Ref. No. 42080 
is listed as an additive in Annex I “Union list” of Commis-
sion Regulation (EU) No. 10/2011 on plastic materials and 
articles intended to come into contact with food. This 
regulation and its amendments are commonly named 
as Plastics Implementing Measure (PIM) and include the 
following specifi cation:
 • Primary particles of 10 - 300 nm, which are aggregated 
to a size of 100 - 1200 nm possibly forming agglomer-
ates within the size distribution of 300 nm – mm
 • Toluene extractables: maximum 0.1 %, determined 
according to ISO method 6209
 • UV absorption of Cyclohexane extract at 386 nm: < 0.02 
AU for a 1 cm cell or < 0.1 AU for a 5 cm cell, determined 
according to a generally recognized method of analysis
 • Benzo(a)pyrene content: maximum 0.25 mg / kg carbon 
black [0.25 ppm]
The Benzo(a)pyrene content is the most critical parame-
ter to carbon black and there is no monitoring method 
defi ned by the EU Commission. Orion Engineered Carbons 
uses GC-MS (gas chromatography with mass spectrometry) 
of a hot extract with toluene according to an established 
FDA procedure.
The following restriction applies to FCM-substance No. 411; 
Ref. No. 42080.
 • Maximum use level of carbon black in polymers:  
2.5 % by weight
2  PAH relevant regulations
2.1 Relevant regulations for plastics directly 
related to the raw material
As a result of the manufacturing process trace quantities of 
PAHs are present in carbon blacks. These contaminants are 
tightly bound to the surface of manufactured carbon black 
and can only be removed after vigorous solvent extraction 
in the laboratory.
2.1.2 Swiss Ordinance 817.023.21
The Swiss Federal Department of Home Aff airs (FDHA) 
issued a revised version of the Ordinance of Materials and 
Articles (SR 817.023.21), which came into force on 1st May 
2017. Article 35 of this section details the requirement that 
only permitted substances should be used in the manufac-
turing auf packaging inks.
The restrictions and specifi cations of substance No. 1194 & 
EC Ref. No. 42080 “carbon black” are laid down in Annex 2 
(plastics), Annex 9 (silicones) an Annex 10 (packaging inks).
The specifi cation in regard to primary particles, toluene 
extractables, UV absorption of Cyclohexane and Benzo(a)
pyrene content ist identical with Commission Regulation 
(EU 10/2011). The carbon black content ist limited for 
polymers with max. 2,5 % but no limitation of carbon black 
content for packaging inks.

of furnace blacks in 1994, but with high requirements on 
purity as follows:

2.2.1 Commission Regulation (EU) No. 1272/2013 
The following listed PAHs are referring to the Commis-
sion Regulation (EU) No. 1272/2013 of 6 December 2013 
amending Annex XVII to Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 of 
the European Parliament and of the Council on the Regis-
tration, Evaluation, Authorization and Restriction of Chemi-
cals (REACH). The required limits (e.g. on PAH), according 
to some voluntary quality standards, apply to the fi nal 
consumer article, which may contain amongst others, only 
a small amount of specialty carbon blacks. 
Orion Engineered Carbons points out, that those standards 
require tests on the fi nal product, which are in the respon-
sibility of the producer of the fi nal product.
Articles made of rubber or plastic components coming into 
direct, prolonged or short-term repetitive contact with the 
human skin or the oral cavity, under normal or reasonably 
foreseeable conditions of use, must not contain more than 
1 mg/kg b.w. of any of the listed PAHs. 
In toys, including activity toys and childcare articles, the 
amount of any listed PAHs need to be below 0.5 mg/kg.

COLOUR BLACK FW 310
水性和溶剂型涂料用超高黑度特种炭黑
技术信息 1485
--- PAGE 2 ---
1  引言
黑、更黑、超级黑！长久以来，如何制造更黑的黑色涂
料是涂料生产商努力追求的方向，特别是在汽车领域。
为了在外观的竞争中脱颖而出，涂料生产商一直致力于
实现汽车厂商要求的终极黑色涂层。不仅如此，高端工业
涂料应用和电子消费品等涂料细分市场也对高黑度炭黑兴
致勃勃，以实现超高黑度涂层。为了满足这一需求，欧励
隆付诸了巨大的努力进行创新，从而呈现出了目前非常优
秀的超高黑度特种炭黑：COLOUR BLACK FW 310。
欧励隆工程炭集团是全球领先的炭黑制造商。欧励隆多
年来一直提供粉状和珠状特种炭黑，这些炭黑产品由原
德固赛(Degussa) 的气黑和炉黑工艺制造，包括未处理产
品和后处理产品，可为涂料行业提供高质量、高色度的
炭黑。新研发的 COLOUR BLACK FW 310 扩展了我们的高
端特种炭黑系列产品，并凸显了我们向客户提供一流产
品的承诺。
2  如何制造适用于超高黑度的特种炭黑？
原生粒径大小不同的炭黑混合物通常具有较低的黑度。
粒径分布宽或粒径分布窄但有较大颗粒形成长尾结构的
炭黑也是如此。我们创新部门经验丰富的技术人员勇于
迎接挑战，利用独特的中试反应器，将聚集体尺寸和原
生粒径尺寸变为几乎单峰分布曲线。 
小粒径的炉法炭黑适用于水性体系。我们的目标是研发
出一款既适用于溶剂型体系也适用于水性体系的炉法炭
黑。为达目标，我们采用了基于炉法的炭黑，并对其
进行特殊后处理。此后处理增加了含氧基团（如羧酸
基团）的数量，从而让表面具有更多的极性。因此，该
炭黑最终既适用于溶剂型体系，也适用于水性体系。这
样，用户仅需购买一种产品，即可满足两种不同的应用
需求。不仅降低了应用的复杂性，更重要的是，同一款
产品可应用在不同领域，如汽车原厂漆 (OEM) 和汽车修
补漆。

3  优异的色彩性能

时，他们首先想要满足的愿望就是炭黑的色彩性能。在
高黑度区域 L*a*b*值通常不能清楚地区分不同炭黑。根
据我们的经验，黑度 MY和色相 dM更适合描述深黑色涂
料。有关如何测量这些值的详细信息，请参见参考文献

3.1. COLOUR BLACK FW 310 在水性体系纯色中的应用
特种炭黑分散如下：为了改善特种炭黑的分散性并稳定
水性研磨浆，我们采用了相当于特种炭黑用量的70% 的
活性润湿剂。适用于此目的的助剂是 TEGO® Dispers 760W 
(Evonik Resource Effi  ciency GmbH, 35% 活性)。在使用实
验室分散机 (Pendraulik LR34 ，圆周速度为10 m/s，持续
5分钟) 对炭黑进行初始润湿后，使用标准实验室震荡机  
(Skandex- Disperser DAS 200 或BA S-20) 和钢珠(3mm) 进
行研磨，并分散一小时。炭黑研磨浆的粘度与水的粘度相
近。研磨细度小于5μm。无树脂炭黑研磨浆中特种炭黑的
浓度为13%。关于分散参数以及选择合适的分散设备和研
磨颗粒的详细建议，请参见参考文献[3]。

从图2可以看出，在测试的水性涂料体系中，COLOUR
BLACK FW 310的黑度比之前同类高黑度特种炭黑
COLOUR BLACK FW 255高出超过10多个点。色相值超过
10表明这是一款非常高蓝相的高黑度炭黑。 
众所周知，高表面积炭黑的最终性能在很大程度上取决于
整体涂料配方，尤其是所使用的助剂。我们对从不同的助
剂供应商处获得的三种不同的助剂进行了测试。对助剂的
选择并非面面俱到，但是具有一定的指导性，因为助剂的
选择很大程度上取决于涂料体系和特种炭黑。已使用对于
炭黑量100%的助剂，炭黑的研磨浆浓度为15%。以与第 3 
页描述相同的方式稀释配漆操作。涂料中最终炭黑浓度为
1.5%。
图 3
分散剂对COLOUR BLACK FW 310在水性单组分聚氨酯系统中性
能的影响
从图3可以看出，选择不同的分散剂可导致在黑度上产生
高达10个点的差异，在色相上产生多达3个点的偏差。从
整体的颜色值（色相+黑度）来看，可能会导致接近15个
点的差异，这在强光下和未经训练的肉眼下都可以清楚地
看出。因此，我们建议每位客户关注整个涂料体系，包
括分散剂、分散剂浓度、 pH值、研磨浆粘度、研磨时间
和能量，以选择合适的条件，最大限度地利用高性能炭
黑。举个类似的例子，如果您想驾驶赛车并赢得冠军，
除了赛车本身外，您还需要拥有优秀的配件组合、性能
良好的轮胎以及汽油等。

产品COLOUR BLACK FW 310 旨在提供超高黑度值和蓝色
相，在水性和溶剂型涂料体系中均可使用。同时必须根据
涂料体系选择合适的助剂。在使用COLOUR BLACK FW 310
的过程中遵循本技术信息中给出的建议，可以满足汽车制
造商的要求，即拥有高蓝相的超高黑度汽车，并为金属涂
料寻找到新的颜色选择。

1  Introduction
Deep, deeper, deepest blackness is the desire especially 
in the automotive world. To diff erentiate from other cars, 
end users and coatings manufacturers strive to achieve 
the ultimate black coatings for their cars. Although auto-
motive is the main driver, further coatings segments like 3C 
coatings and high class industrial applications are also very 
interested in carbon blacks that can achieve ultra-high 
jetness. Following this demand, Orion Engineered Carbons 
has put huge eff orts in innovation work, and thus presents 
our currently best in class high blackness carbon black: 
COLOUR BLACK FW 310.
COLOUR BLACK FW 310  extends our portfolio of specialty 
carbon blacks at the upper level and underlines our com-
mitment to deliver to our customer best in class products. 
Orion Engineered Carbons has been off ering over many 
years specialty carbon blacks in powder and for beaded 
forms that are manufactured by the Degussa gas black 
and the furnace black process to produce high quality 
high color carbon blacks for the coatings industry. Orion 
Engineered Carbons is the sole manufacturer of high color 
gas blacks and high color furnace blacks, both untreated 
and after-treated. This off ers the unique opportunity to 
select the right pigment for any application based on 
diff erent chemical behavior.
2  How to achieve a specialty carbon black suitable for ultra-high jetness?
Mixtures of fi ne and coarse carbon blacks typically give low 
jetness performance. Same is true for carbon blacks with 
a broad particle size distribution or with a narrow particle 
size distribution in combination with a long tail of some 
coarser particles. The experienced technicians in our inno-
vation department met the challenge, working with our 
unique pilot reactor on bringing the aggregate size and 
the primary particle size to a nearly mono-modal curve.
Furnace blacks with very fi ne particle size are typically 
suit-able for water-borne systems. Our target was to have a 
pigment based on a furnace black that is suitable for both 
solvent- and water-borne systems. To reach this target we 
took the furnace base black and gave it a special after-
treatment. This after-treatment enhances the amount of 
oxygen containing groups (e.g. carboxylic groups) and 
thus gives the surface more polarity. So the pigment suits 
fi nally to both solvent- and water-borne systems. This ena-
bles customers to purchase one single grade that can be 
used in both applications. Complexity can be reduced, and, 
even more important, the same product can be used e.g. in 
automotive OEM and automotive refi nish products, where 
diff erent solvents are used.
2 OEC-TI 1485-10/ 2022
--- PAGE 3 ---
3  Outstanding coloristic performance
The fi rst desire of coatings customers looking at a pigment 
like COLOUR BLACK FW 310 is the coloristic performance. In 
this high jetness area L*a*b* values are typically not giving 
good diff erentiation of diff erent pigments. According to our 
experience, jetness MY and undertone dM are much better 
to describe deep black coatings. Details, how to measure 
these values, are given in literature [1] and [2].

In order to improve the dispersion of the specialty carbon
black powders and stabilize the water-borne mill bases, 70 %
of active wetting agent related to the specialty carbon 
black powders was used. A suitable additive for this purpose
is TEGO® Dispers 760W (Evonik Resource Effi  ciency GmbH,

carbon blacks in the binder-free millbases was 13 %. More 
detailed recommendations regarding dispersion parameters 
and selecting the right dispersion equipment and milling 
beads can be found in literature [3].

As it is well known that the performance of high surface

tion and especially on the additive in use, we tested three 
diff erent additives from diff erent additive suppliers. The 
selection of the additives is not intended to be exhaustive,

Figure 3 shows that the additives can give up to 10 point 
deviation in jetness and up to three points deviation in 
undertone. Looking at the whole color perception, this can 
result in close to a 15 point diff erence, which is clearly vis-
ible under bright light as well by the untrained human eye. 
Thus we recommend to every customer to look at the whole 
coating system including, additive, additive concentration, 
pH value, mill base viscosity, grinding time and energy to 
select the right conditions to get the utmost out of the 
high performance pigment. An analog to describe this is 
that if you want to drive a racing car, you need besides the 
car itself a great team, good tires, good gasoline, etc. to 
win the championship.

Best Practices for using Micronized Wax 
Micro Powders’ products can elevate your coating formulations from good to great when used 
correctly. It is important to understand the proper techniques to use when incorporating micronized 
powders into a coating. In order to successfully “wet” the wax particles, the liquid used requires 
a lower surface tension than the surface energy of the wax. The term “wet” or “wetting” refers to 
completely dispersing individual micro-fine particles into a liquid medium. 
It is generally recommended to avoid adding micronized wax directly into the final liquid 
formulation, as this typically will lead to poor wetting, insufficient dispersion, agglomerated wax 
particles, coating defects, and poor end use performance. It is usually difficult to wet out a small 
percentage of dry wax in a large batch of liquid material. Ideally, a concentrated dispersion is first 
prepared using the wax powder and one or more components of the coating formulation. Then the 
appropriate amount of this pre-dispersion is added to the final coating. If there is a grind step in the 
manufacturing process, the dry wax can be incorporated at that stage. In solvent based formulations, 
it is important to monitor the grind temperature so it does not exceed the melting point of the wax.
For customers who would rather not handle dry powders, many of our products are available as 
pourable, aqueous Microspersions® which can be easily added at any stage of manufacturing. A 
selection of products are shown on page 10, and referenced throughout the brochure with .
For more information, please refer to our How to Disperse Micronized Waxes guide, which provides 
detailed information on dispersing micronized wax powders into a variety of systems, including: 
solvent based, water based, energy curable, and 100% solids and reactive systems.

INTRODUCTION
Micro Powders manufactures micronized wax powders, many of which are based on polymers that have low surface 
energies. It is important to understand the proper techniques to use when incorporating micronized powders into 
a coating. To successfully “wet” the wax particles, the liquid used requires a lower surface tension than the surface 
energy of the wax. The term “wet” or “wetting” refers to completely dispersing individual micro-fine particles into a 
liquid medium.
¡	Solvent based
¡ Water based
¡ Energy curable
¡ 100% solids and reactive systems
GENERAL CONCEPT
It is generally recommended to avoid adding micronized wax directly into the final liquid formulation, as this typically 
will lead to poor wetting, insufficient dispersion, agglomerated wax particles, coating defects, and poor end use 
performance. It is usually difficult to wet out a small percentage of dry wax in a large batch of liquid material. Ideally, 
a concentrated dispersion is first prepared using the wax powder and one or more components of the coating 
formulation. The appropriate amount of this pre-dispersion is then added to the final coating.
UNDERSTANDING WAX DENSITY
The density of a wax additive affects how the wax behaves once dispersed into a liquid. If the density of the wax is 
lower than the density of the liquid, the wax will want to rise to the surface and float. If the density of the wax is higher 
than the density of the liquid, the wax will want to sink to the bottom. Examples:
Wax Type Density Formula Type Result
Polypropylene 0.89 Water based (density 1.0) Float
Carnauba Wax 1.00 Water based (density 1.0) Stable
PTFE 2.20 Water based (density 1.0) Sink
Viscosity will affect the rate of this flotation or settling; higher viscosity systems will respond more slowly than lower 
viscosity systems. Formulators should be aware of this when preparing pre-dispersed wax compounds since the 
homogeneity of the dispersed wax can change over time.
DISPERSION TECHNIQUE
For best results, it is recommended to use a high speed impeller disk 
such as a ConnBlade type ITT to provide sufficient shear energy to wet 
and disperse the wax and to break down any agglomerates that may be 
generated during the dispersion process. The effective shear energy is 
dependent on the shear rate and viscosity. Using an impeller disk that 
provides pumping action will give circulation of the total mass and wet 
out the particles more thoroughly.
In the laboratory, dispersion of dry wax can be achieved with a disk tip speed of 1,000 – 1,500 feet per minute (FPM), 
or around 5 – 7 meters per second (m/s). In a production environment, a tip speed of 4,000 – 5,000 FPM, or around 
22 – 26 m/s, is a good target.
Our product recommendations take this phenomenon into account to recommend the best product for your specific 
application (where possible). Many of our newer products have been designed with densities slightly over 1.0 to 
optimize in-can stability in most types of coating systems.

SOLVENT BASED SYSTEMS
Since the surface tension of solvent based liquids is typically low, it is relatively easy to disperse micronized wax 
powders into these types of formulations. Although it may be more efficient to prepare a concentrated pre-dispersion 
using one or more of the solvent based formula components, it may also be possible (with efficient mixing) to add 
micronized waxes directly into the final coating.

As the wax is dispersed, the viscosity of the mixture will decrease, and the final dispersed material will have a glossy 
appearance. Add the appropriate amount of this pre-dispersion to provide the addition level you desire in your coating.
WATER BASED SYSTEMS
Since the surface tension of water based liquids is high, it can be difficult to disperse micronized wax powders directly 
into these types of formulations. It is highly recommended that a concentrated pre-dispersion be prepared using one 
or more of the water based formula components.

It is important to note that when dispersing a micronized wax (especially grades based on lower melting polymers 
such as synthetic wax or carnauba wax) into a solvent based formulation, the formulator should use caution so as not 
to soften or dissolve the wax.
Overheating the dispersion can cause the micronized wax to become soluble and possibly recrystallize as it is cooled 
to room temperature. The dispersion temperature should be kept below 40 °C (104 °F) to prevent it from dissolving. 
Also, the use of aromatic or other strong solvents can lead to similar issues with dissolution and recrystallization, 
so avoid these solvents where possible with lower melting waxes. In fact, many solvent based coating formulators 
prefer to avoid lower melting wax grades because of these potential production issues, instead opting for a more 
temperature-robust polyethylene wax additive.

appearance. Add the appropriate amount of this pre-dispersion to provide the addition level you desire in your coating.
For further information on extending shelf stability of a waterbased wax dispersion, please read “How to Stabilize a 
Water Based Wax Dispersion” at the end of this guide.

ENERGY CURABLE SYSTEMS
Follow the procedure and formula for solvent based systems, replacing the solvent component with monomer and/ 
or oligomer from the energy curable formula. Then add the appropriate amount of this pre-dispersion to provide the 
addition level you desire in your coating. Use caution during the dispersion process to avoid excessive shear and/or 
heat development that may cause the energy curable materials to be affected.
100% SOLIDS & REACTIVE SYSTEMS
Follow the procedure and formula for solvent based systems, replacing the solvent component with a low viscosity 
component from the 100% solids formula. Low reactivity diluents such as polyaldimine or exempt solvents such as 
propylene carbonate are useful in preparing pre-dispersions. Then add the appropriate amount of this pre-dispersion 
to provide the addition level you desire in your coating.
HOW TO VERIFY A WELL-DISPERSED WAX
It is relatively easy to check a coating or pre-dispersion to ensure that the wax particles have been fully dispersed and 
wetted out. A grind gauge such as a NPIRI gauge is the easiest way to evaluate the material. Micro Powders wax 
products have a NPIRI gauge specification that you can use as a reference point. Other gauges such as a Hegman may 
also be useful in confirming the degree of dispersion. Of course, the best way to check will be to prepare a laboratory 
scale batch of your coating and evaluate the dried film for surface uniformity, gloss level, COF, or other surface property 
measurements.
HOW TO STABILIZE A WATER BASED WAX DISPERSION
As discussed earlier, many micronized wax grades will float in a water based system because the particle density is 
lower than that of water (1.0). This flotation process occurs faster in lower viscosity systems. To slow this process, 
the viscosity of a wax dispersion can be increased through the incorporation of a thickening agent. Polyacrylic acid 
thickening agents or xanthan gum can be used.
DEFOAMING
If the wax dispersion process generates excessive foam, a defoamer can be added, typically at 0.5%.  Rhodoline® 643 
(Solvay) is an effective defoaming agent for water based wax dispersions.
THE MICROSPERSION® OPTION
If your application is water based, and you would prefer to purchase pre-dispersed wax in an aqueous liquid form, 
Micro Powders offers many of our most popular products in Microspersion® form. These high solids nonionic wax 
dispersions are easy to add directly to your final waterbased formulation.  
HAVING PROBLEMS?
Micro Powders’ Technical Support Staff are just a phone call or e-mail away and are always available to help. If you are 
facing challenges with your application and need our assistance, please contact us.

INTRODUCTION
Coating formulators now have the ability to modify the tactile 
surface properties of their products with MicroTouch.  Based 
on aliphatic polyurethane technology, MicroTouch additives 
are micron-sized elastic particles that distort when disturbed by 
a physical force (such as finger touch or abrasive action) and 
then return to their original spherical shape when the force is 
removed. These products can be used in combination with many 
different types of coating resins to achieve effects that range from 
satiny smooth to leathery to rubbery. MicroTouch additives are 
highly resilient particles that can be used to modify and enhance 
the feel of a coating surface. These additives will provide a 
matte appearance as well as superior scratch, burnish, and mar 
resistance. MicroTouch additives are available in several particle 
sizes, each of which brings different tactile properties. MicroTouch 
additives are an ideal alternative to formaldehyde-based materials 
such as polyureas. 
MicroTouch additives will improve chemical resistance and 
hydrolytic stability. Taber abrasion resistance can be dramatically 
improved with an addition of 2-3% of MicroTouch. 
MicroTouch additives can be used to modify coatings designed for 
plastics, metals, paper, wood, leather, and other textiles.  Common 
industrial applications include electronics (computers, laptops, 
mobile phones), automotive interiors, wall coverings, parquet 
and vinyl flooring, inks, and furniture. 
FORMULATION NOTES
It is important to understand that the ultimate “feel” of a coating 
formulated with MicroTouch is highly dependent on the choice  
of resin system. Harder resin systems formulated with MicroTouch 
will provide a surface with a smooth, satiny feel. Softer resin systems 
can provide surfaces that have a rubbery, anti-slip feel. Lower 
percentages (2-6%) of MicroTouch will provide gloss reduction and 
MicroTouch
Soft Touch Coating Additives
abrasion resistance with limited tactile effects. At higher percentages 
(6-10%), more pronounced tactile properties can be achieved. 
The formulated examples presented in this brochure demonstrate 
some of the tactile effects that can be achieved by combining 
MicroTouch additives with different types of coating resins.  These 
examples should not be considered as fully formulated commercial 
coatings.  They are presented strictly to show the range of soft 
touch effects that can be achieved.
PROCESSING NOTES
MicroTouch additives are virtually indestructible and are easy to 
incorporate into coatings with an impeller disk disperser such as 
a Conn ITT blade (or similar).  A tip speed of around 3-3.5 m/s 
should be sufficient to wet and disperse the product into a coating. 
In solvent based systems, additional shear energy may be required 
to disperse and deagglomerate the product. 
HIGH TEMPERATURE AND SOLVENT BASED 
APPLICATIONS 
MicroTouch additives are suitable for applications with curing 
temperatures up to100-120 °C. For applications in the120-140 °C 
range, the products may show some yellowing. Applications 
exceeding 140 °C are not recommended as the particles will swell 
and/or stick together.
MicroTouch additives will swell and absorb solvent if slurried 
directly into alcohol (ethanol, isopropanol) or other highly polar 
solvents.  They should instead be dispersed into the alcohol based 
resin system to disperse and stabilize the particles.
MicroTouch additives should not be used in coating systems 
based on dimethylformamide (DMF) as the particles will swell 
significantly.

MicroTouch additives are spherical aliphatic polyurethane 
particles that can be used in combination with many 
different types of coating resins to achieve effects that range 
from satiny smooth to leathery to rubbery. MicroTouch 
additives are highly resilient particles that will provide a 
matte appearance as well as superior burnish and mar 
resistance. Available in several particle sizes, each MicroTouch 
additive brings different tactile properties. MicroTouch 
additives are an ideal alternative to formaldehyde-based 
materials such as polyureas.
MicroTouch additives can improve chemical resistance and
hydrolytic stability. Taber abrasion resistance can be 
dramatically improved with an addition of 2-3% of 
MicroTouch. MicroTouch additives can be used to modify 
coatings for plastics, metals, paper, wood, leather and 
other textiles.
Formulation Notes
It is important to understand that the ultimate “feel” of a 
coating formulated with MicroTouch is highly dependent
on the choice of resin system. Harder, higher Tg resin 
systems formulated with MicroTouch will provide a surface 
with a silky, satiny feel (2-6% dosage). Softer, lower Tg 
resin systems can provide surfaces that have a rubbery, 
anti-slip feel (6 -12% dosage).

MODIFY YOUR TACTILE SURFACE PROPERTIES
WITH MICROTOUCH.
In UV coatings, a rubbery soft touch effect can be achieved 
by starting with a UV adhesive formula and modifying with 
enough MicroTouch to provide a tack-free surface above the 
soft, flexible cured adhesive layer. 
The formulated examples presented in this brochure 
demonstrate some of the tactile effects that can be
achieved by combining MicroTouch additives with 
different types of coating resins.
High Temperature and 
Solvent-Based Applications
MicroTouch additives are suitable for applications with curing 
temperatures up to 100 -120°C. For application in the 120-140°C 
range, the products may show some yellowing. Applications 
exceeding 140°C are not recommended as the particles will 
swell and/or stick together. 
MicroTouch additives will swell and absorb solvent if slurried 
directly into alcohol (ethanol, isopropanol) or other highly polar 
solvents. They should instead be dispersed into the 
alcohol-based resin system to wet and stabilize the particles. 
MicroTouch additives should not be used in coating systems 
based on dimethylformamide (DMF) as the particles will 
swell significantly.

PolyGlide 1226XF 
Introduction 
PolyGlide 1226XF is a micronized composite wax based on high density polyethylene 
(HDPE) that has been modified with two different types of high performance ceramic.  The 
ceramic components significantly improve abrasion resistance and enhance the inherent 
lubricity of the HDPE without the use of PTFE. 
PolyGlide 1226XF can be compared to MPP-611XF (same polyethylene wax without ceramic 
modification), and can also be evaluated as a PTFE-free alternative to Polyfluo 150:

Introduction 
AquaMatte 22, AquaMatte 31, and AquaMatte 26HD are a series of micronized oxidized polyethylene 
waxes designed for gloss reduction and stability in waterborne systems. PropylMatte 31HD is micronized 
polypropylene that is designed for use as a matting agent.   
PropylMatte 31HD and AquaMatte 26HD have been density -modified to 1.07 g/cc to eliminate wax 
flotation, especially in water based and UV/EB systems.  
 
Objectives 
Compare the matting efficiency and coefficient of friction (COF) using AquaMatte 22, AquaMatte 31, 
AquaMatte 26HD and PropylMatte 31HD.   
Study Methodology 
Aqueous polyurethane dispersions were made at a 1%, 2%, 3%, 4% and 5% dosage (based on total 
formula weight) for each product. The dispersions were drawn down using a 0.003” (76 μm) Bird 
applicator.  Panels were dried for one week before measurements were taken. 
Specular gloss was measured at 20°, 60° and 85° on the black area of a coated lacquered Lenet a Chart 
Form 2A. 
COF was measured using a Kayeness Model D1055 tester.  A Leneta card, coated with the cured test 
material, is secured to the moving platform.  A digital force gauge attaches directly to a 200 gram sled 
which sits on the Leneta card.  The cured coating is affixed to the sled.  The platform moves at a rate of 0.1 
inches per second.  The force gauge measures the gram-force load and determines static and kinetic COF.

MPP- 611AL 
Introduction 
MPP-611 is one of Micro Powders’ most popular additives for coatings requiring excellent 
rub and mar resistance with good surface slip, and anti -blocking properties. MPP-611AL is 
a micronized composite based on high density polyethylene reinforced with 300 nm 
aluminum oxide nanoparticles (Mohs Hardness 9.).

Objective 
Compare the level of scratch resistance between MPP-611XF and MPP-611AL. 
 
Study Methodology 
Pencil scratch tests were conducted on a water based polyurethane coating:

The polyurethane coating was dosed with 1% of MPP -611XF and MPP -611AL. Coatings 
were drawn down with a #28 wire wound rod to produce approximately 1 mil DFT coatings. 
Coatings were dried for 7 days at room temperature and ~50% humidity. 
 
The pencil scratch hardness test was conducted under controlled measurement conditions 
using a Taber Linear Abraser.

Revision 07/2024 - Page 2 of 4        
 
Taber Linear Abraser – Pencil Scratch Test Instrument 
 
The motion of the abrasion is linear - one cycle is equal to one forward and one backward 
stroke of the test arm. The Taber Linear Abraser 5750, coupled with the Pencil Hardness 
kit accessory, enables controlled and reproducible Pencil Scratch Hardness tes ting of 
coatings by allowing the user to control the amount of force applied during the 
measurement, the number of linear cycles, the stroke length, as well as the speed. For 
this particular study, a force of 5.3 Newtons (equivalent to 536 g) was applied during the 
stroke. The stroke length was set to 0.5 inches and the speed was set to 2 cycles per 
minute. Each coating was scratched for one-half of a cycle (in the forward motion, as 
specified in ASTM D3363). These specific test conditions allowed one to observe 
differences in the amount of scratch for each dosed and undosed coating. Pencil scratch 
was assessed visually by comparing the surfaces of the scratched coatings and assigning 
the scratch hardness rating.

1402 – A Comparison of Printing Ink Rub Resistance 
Using Synthetic and Polyethylene Waxes 
 
Introduction 
Micro Powders offers several gr ades of s ynthetic wax and p olyethylene wax to the coatings a nd inks 
markets. These finely micronized additives will improve rub resistance, with the level of improvement a 
function of the nature of the polymer used. The following wax additives will be compared: 
 
 
Product: Description: Mean particle size, μm: Maximum particle size, μm: 
MPP-230VF Lower MW polyethylene 11 maximum 31 
MPP-620F Medium MW polyethylene 7-9 31 
MPP-635F Higher MW polyethylene 8-10 31 
MP-22 Synthetic Wax 8-10 31  
 
Objective 
Compare the efficiency in rub resistance improvement with a r ange of wax ad ditives hav ing similar 
particle size distribution but different wax chemistry. 
 
 
Study Methodology 
The test formula for this study was an acr ylic waterbased black printing ink that contained no wax 
additives. Each wax additive was dosed and fully dispersed at a 1% level based on total formula weight. 
The modified ink samples were dra wn do wn on se aled Leneta cards using a #10 wire wound rod and 
allowed to dry for 1 week at ambient conditions before testing. A #10 w ire wound 
rod applies a wet film thickness of approximately 0.01” (25.6 μm). 
 
A Su therland Rub tester was us ed to abrade  the test pan els. The tester is a motor 
driven instrument that moves a weighted test strip over a printed specimen through 
an arc.  The 4 p ound (1.8 kg) weight was used.  Each p anel was tested on t he 
Sutherland by abra ding the p rinted sur face ag ainst white unsealed Lene ta card. 
Panels were abraded for 50 and 200 cycles.

New Product Performance Study – MicroKlear 418AL 
Introduction 
MicroKlear 418 is one of Micro Powders’ most popular additives for coatings requiring improved surface 
slip and scratch resistance with excellent clarity and gloss retention.   MicroKlear 418AL is a micronized 
composite based on carnauba wax  reinforced with 300 nm aluminum oxide nanoparticles (Mohs 
Hardness 9). 
 
Property: MKL-418 MKL-418AL

Maximum particle size (µm) 22.0 22.0 
Melting point (°C) 81 – 86 81 – 86 
Density at 25 °C (g/cc) 0.99 1.04 
 
Objective 
Compare the level of scratch resistance between MicroKlear 418 and MicroKlear 418AL. 
 
Study Methodology 
Pencil scratch tests were conducted on a water based polyurethane coating: 
 
Formula: Weight %: 
  UROTUF® L522-W-40 (Reichhold) 89.6 
  Diethylene glycol monoethyl ether 5.0 
BYK-345 0.5

The polyurethane coating was dosed with 1% of MK 418 and MK 418AL. Coatings were drawn down with 
a #28 wire wound rod to produce approx imately 1 mil DFT coatings . Coatings were dried for 7  days at 
room temperature and ~50% humidity. 
 
The pencil scratch hardness test was conducted under controlled measurement conditions using a Taber 
Linear Abraser.

--- PAGE 2 ---

Taber Linear Abraser – Pencil Scratch Test Instrument 
 
The motion of the abrasion is linear - one cycle is equal to one forward and one backward stroke of the 
test arm. The Taber Linear Abraser  5750, coupled with the Pencil Hardness kit accessory, enables 
controlled and reproducible Pencil Scratch Hardness testing of coatings by allowing the user to control 
the amount of force applied during the measurement, the number of linear cycles, the stroke length, as 
well as the speed. For this particular study, a force of 5.3 Newtons (equivalent to 536 g) was applied 
during the stroke. The stroke length was set to 0.5 inches and the speed was set to 2 cycles per minute. 
Each coating was scratched for one-half of a cycle (in the forward motion, as specified in ASTM D3363). 
These specific test conditions allowed one to observe differences in the amount of scratch for each 
dosed and undosed coating. Pencil scratch was assessed visually by comparing the surfaces of the 
scratched coatings and assigning the scratch hardness rating.

MicroMatte 1415-EZ is a micronized composite wax based on modified synthetic wax . The 
composite components significantly improve dirt pick up resistance  (DPUR), abrasion 
resistance, burnish resistance, and scratch resistance, while also enhancing slip and lubricity.  
MicroMatte 1415-EZ can be compared to other popular additives for architectural coatings.

1501 - A Comparison of Matting Efficiency and  
COF Using AquaMatte® 22, AquaMatte 26HD,  
AquaMatte 31 and PropylMatte 31HD 
 
Introduction 
AquaMatte 22, AquaMatte 31, and AquaMatte 26HD are a series of micronized oxidized polyethylene 
waxes designed for gloss reduction and stability in waterborne systems. PropylMatte 31HD is micronized 
polypropylene that is designed for use as a matting agent.   
PropylMatte 31HD and AquaMatte 26HD have been density -modified to 1.07 g/cc to eliminate wax 
flotation, especially in water based and UV/EB systems.  
 
Objectives 
Compare the matting efficiency and coefficient of friction (COF) using AquaMatte 22, AquaMatte 31, 
AquaMatte 26HD and PropylMatte 31HD.   
Study Methodology 
Aqueous polyurethane dispersions were made at a 1%, 2%, 3%, 4% and 5% dosage (based on total 
formula weight) for each product. The dispersions were drawn down using a 0.003” (76 μm) Bird 
applicator.  Panels were dried for one week before measurements were taken. 
Specular gloss was measured at 20°, 60° and 85° on the black area of a coated lacquered Lenet a Chart 
Form 2A. 
COF was measured using a Kayeness Model D1055 tester.  A Leneta card, coated with the cured test 
material, is secured to the moving platform.  A digital force gauge attaches directly to a 200 gram sled 
which sits on the Leneta card.  The cured coating is affixed to the sled.  The platform moves at a rate of 0.1 
inches per second.  The force gauge measures the gram-force load and determines static and kinetic COF.

Objective

Study Methodology 
Aqueous polyurethane dispersions were made at a 0.5%, 1.0% and 1.5% dosages (based on total formula 
weight) for each product. The dispersions were drawn down using a 0.003” (76 μm) Bird applicator on a 
coated lacquered Leneta Chart Form 2A. Panels were dried for one week before measurements were taken. 
 
A Taber Abraser was used following ASTM D4060. The weight loss was measured in milligrams and 
recorded after 1000 cycles using 1000 gram auxiliary masses on each CS-17 wheel.

      PRODUCT PERFORMANCE STUDY 
MicroTex® 950 
Introduction 
 
MicroTex 950 is a PFAS- free additive that provides fine textur ing and low gloss in 
powder coatings.  The performance of MicroTex 950 can be compared to PTFE-based 
texturing additives such as Fluo 750TX: 
 
Physical Property: MicroTex 950 Fluo 750TX 
Wax Type Modified polyolefin PTFE 
Melting Point °C 135 - 140 >325 
Density @ 25 °C (g/cc) 1.22 2.20 
Maximum particle size (µm) 74 145 
 
Objective 
To evaluate the performance of MicroTex 950 vs. PTFE in various powder coating 
systems. 
 
Test Methods 
 
• Specular Gloss (ASTM D2457) 
• Impact Resistance (ASTM D2794) 
• Conical Mandrel Bend (ASTM D522) 
• Crosshatch Adhesion (ASTM D3359) 
• Pellet Flow (ASTM D3541) 
 
General Formulation Guidance 
Recommended loading level for MicroTex 950 is  4.0 – 6.0% by total formula weight 
to achieve the optimal effect. Lower levels may reduce gloss and improve edge 
coverage but will not form a texture. Too high of a level may restrict the flow of the 
coating and result in a discontinuous film. 
 
MicroTex 950 is added at the premix stage and homogenized with the rest of the raw 
materials in the extruder. The material has a low bulk density, so the feed rate may 
need to be increased to achieve the same throughput as a powder formulation without 
the additive. 
 
Because the texture formation is a physical phenomenon that occurs  during curing, 
MicroTex 950 can be used in any powder coating binder chemistry and is independent 
of cure temperature.

Pellet Flow 
Pellet flow is a test of melt/flow under low shear. In general, a longer pellet corresponds 
to a smoother coating.  A shorter pellet has limited flow but better edge coverage.  
 
 
 
Mechanical Properties 
 
• MicroTex 950 did not influence adhesion to the substrate 
• At a 6% loading level, the impact resistance of the coatings was slightly lower 
vs. the PTFE-containing control for the TGIC and HAA formulas, but was slightly 
higher in the hybrid system 
• The mandrel bend flexibility of the coatings was not affected 
• Pellet flows were similar in the hybrid and TGIC systems, and were reduced in 
the HAA system

Guidance for White Formulations 
 
Here are some comments on how to get best results in a white powder system: 
1. The ratio by volume of the additive to the binder changes depending on the 
specific gravity of the fillers and pigments. The density of the barium sulfate 
used in our study is close to titanium dioxide, which would be used in a white  
formulation.  However, there could be a big difference if the additive is in at a 
constant weight but you change 30% of the formula from calcium carbonate 
(specific gravity = 2.7) to TiO2 (specific gravity = 4.2). 
2. Texturing performance could be impacted  when using a resin with low melt 
viscosity and low glass transition temperature. If MicroTex 950 is  added to an 
otherwise very smooth and high gloss starting formula, the rheological effect 
will not be as pronounced. 
3. The inert (filler and pigment) portion of the formula could have different oil 
absorption values. In this case, higher oil absorption would increase the 
texturing effect. This could also be affected by differences in particle size of the 
mineral fillers.
